items.definition: vague, unclear, or not well defined
items.explanation: From Latin nebula, 'cloud'. It is often used for ideas, plans, or memories.
items.example: Her plans for the future were still nebulous, with no dates or details.
items.picture_idea: A hazy cloud of mist hiding the outline of a shape

items.definition: wicked or criminal
items.example: The detective uncovered the villain's nefarious scheme to steal the museum's treasures.
items.picture_idea: A shadowy figure in a cloak sneaking through a dark room

items.definition: calm and relaxed, as if not worried or interested
items.explanation: Comes from French. It can describe someone who seems casual even in an exciting or tense moment.
items.example: He gave a nonchalant shrug when they announced he had won.
items.picture_idea: A person shrugging with a relaxed smile

items.definition: a small, subtle difference in meaning, tone, or color
items.example: A good translator must understand the nuances of both languages.
items.picture_idea: Two nearly identical shades of blue side by side

items.definition: to make something unclear or hard to understand
items.explanation: Often used when someone confuses a topic on purpose, such as with complicated wording.
items.example: The company tried to obfuscate the problem with long, technical reports.
items.picture_idea: A person hiding a page of text behind swirling smoke

items.definition: showy in a way meant to impress others
items.example: The millionaire's ostentatious mansion had gold fountains on the lawn.
items.picture_idea: A huge mansion with gold fountains and a fancy car

items.definition: suggesting that something bad is about to happen
items.example: Dark, ominous clouds gathered above the picnic.
items.picture_idea: Black storm clouds rolling over an empty field

items.definition: a typical model or pattern; a way of thinking about something
items.explanation: In science, a 'paradigm shift' is a big change in how people understand a subject.
items.example: The discovery of germs caused a paradigm shift in medicine.

items.definition: harmful in a slow, hidden way
items.example: Rumors can have a pernicious effect on a friendship.
items.picture_idea: A weed slowly strangling a healthy plant

items.definition: the pleasant smell of rain falling on dry ground
items.explanation: The word was coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists, from Greek petra 'stone' and ichor, the fluid in the veins of the gods.
items.example: We opened the windows to enjoy the petrichor after the first storm of summer.
items.picture_idea: Raindrops hitting dry, dusty earth

items.definition: a large amount, more than is needed
items.explanation: Usually used in the phrase 'a plethora of'.
items.example: The menu offered a plethora of choices, so it took her ages to decide.
items.picture_idea: A table overflowing with many different dishes

items.definition: a cure or solution that is said to fix all problems
items.explanation: Often used in negative sentences, such as 'there is no panacea'.
items.example: Technology is not a panacea for every problem in schools.
items.picture_idea: A magic bottle labeled 'cures everything'

items.definition: dealing with things in a practical, sensible way
items.example: Taking a pragmatic approach, she chose the cheaper option that still worked well.
items.picture_idea: A person comparing two tools and choosing the useful one

items.definition: idealistic in a way that is not realistic or practical
items.explanation: From Don Quixote, the hero of a Spanish novel who fought windmills thinking they were giants.
items.example: His quixotic plan to plant a forest in the desert amazed everyone.
items.picture_idea: A knight on a horse charging at a windmill

items.definition: a state of not knowing what to do in a difficult situation
items.example: She was in a quandary over which invitation to accept.
items.picture_idea: A person standing at a fork in the road scratching their head

items.definition: stubbornly refusing to obey or cooperate
items.example: The recalcitrant mule would not move, no matter how hard we pulled.
items.picture_idea: A mule planting its feet while a person tugs the rope

items.definition: unwilling to share thoughts or feelings; reserved
items.example: He was reticent about his past and rarely spoke of his childhood.
items.picture_idea: A person with a finger to their lips

items.definition: able to recover quickly from difficulty or to spring back into shape
items.example: Children are often more resilient than adults expect.
items.picture_idea: A bent branch springing back upright

items.definition: a happy accident; finding something good by chance
items.explanation: Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754 from a fairy tale, 'The Three Princes of Serendip'.
items.example: It was pure serendipity that we met on the same train.
items.picture_idea: A person happily finding a coin on the pavement

items.definition: a person who flatters important people to gain favor
items.example: The king was surrounded by sycophants who agreed with everything he said.
items.picture_idea: A group of people bowing and clapping around a king

items.definition: more than is needed; unnecessary
items.example: The editor cut every superfluous word from the article.
items.picture_idea: A red pen crossing out extra words on a page

items.definition: calm and showing no emotion when facing pain or trouble
items.explanation: From Stoicism, an ancient Greek philosophy that taught people to stay calm and accept what they cannot change.
items.example: She remained stoic as the doctor explained the long recovery.
items.picture_idea: A calm person standing in heavy rain without flinching

items.definition: false or fake, though made to look real
items.explanation: Often used for claims, arguments, or evidence that sound right but are not.
items.example: The scientist rejected the spurious claim because it had no evidence.
items.picture_idea: A magnifying glass revealing a fake signature

items.definition: happening now and then, not regularly
items.example: Sporadic showers fell throughout the afternoon.
items.picture_idea: A few scattered raindrops falling from a mostly clear sky

items.definition: holding on firmly; refusing to give up
items.example: The tenacious climber kept going despite the freezing wind.
items.picture_idea: A climber gripping a cliff face with determination

items.definition: saying very little; quiet by nature
items.example: The old fisherman was taciturn and spoke only when necessary.
items.picture_idea: An old man sitting silently by a boat

items.definition: a feeling of fear or worry about something that may happen
items.example: She opened the exam paper with trepidation.
items.picture_idea: A nervous person peeking through half-closed fingers at a door

items.definition: able to be touched or clearly seen to be real
items.explanation: The opposite is 'intangible'. Tangible results are results you can clearly see.
items.example: The project produced tangible results: three new classrooms.
items.picture_idea: A hand touching a solid object

items.definition: seeming to be everywhere at once
items.explanation: From Latin ubique, 'everywhere'.
items.example: Smartphones have become ubiquitous in modern life.
items.picture_idea: A crowd of people all looking at phones

items.definition: clear and firm, with no doubt
items.example: The judge gave an unequivocal answer: the rule applied to everyone.
items.picture_idea: A person firmly pointing and nodding

items.definition: to take power or a position by force or without the right
items.example: The prince's uncle tried to usurp the throne.
items.picture_idea: A man snatching a crown from a king's head

items.definition: to treat with great respect and honor
items.example: Many cultures venerate their elders for their wisdom.
items.picture_idea: Young people bowing respectfully to an elderly person

items.definition: felt or experienced through someone else rather than yourself
items.example: He got vicarious pleasure from watching his sister's travel videos.
items.picture_idea: A person at home smiling while watching a friend's trip on a screen

items.definition: a small trace of something that once existed
items.example: Only a few vestiges of the ancient wall remain.
items.picture_idea: A crumbling stone fragment of an old wall in a field

items.definition: likely to change suddenly or become violent; evaporating quickly
items.explanation: Used for tempers, markets, and situations, and in chemistry for liquids that turn to gas easily.
items.example: The volatile situation could turn violent at any moment.
items.picture_idea: A bubbling flask with vapor rising quickly

items.definition: to clear someone of blame or show that they were right
items.example: The new evidence vindicated the accused man.
items.picture_idea: A person being declared innocent in a courtroom

items.definition: to gradually become smaller, weaker, or less
items.explanation: Used for the moon when it shows less of its face each night. The opposite is 'wax'.
items.example: Her interest in the hobby began to wane after a few months.
items.picture_idea: The moon shrinking from full to a thin crescent

items.definition: playful and unusual in a charming way
items.example: The garden had whimsical statues of frogs wearing hats.
items.picture_idea: A frog statue wearing a tiny top hat in a garden

items.definition: feeling a quiet, sad longing for something
items.example: He gave a wistful smile as he looked at old photographs.
items.picture_idea: A person gazing out a window holding an old photo

items.definition: dislike or fear of people from other countries or cultures
items.explanation: From Greek xenos 'stranger' and phobos 'fear'.
items.example: The campaign aimed to fight xenophobia by celebrating cultural diversity.

items.definition: a wooden bar that joins two animals so they can pull a load together; something that oppresses
items.explanation: Figuratively, 'the yoke of tyranny' means harsh control over people.
items.example: The oxen wore a heavy wooden yoke as they pulled the plow.
items.picture_idea: Two oxen joined by a wooden bar pulling a plow

items.definition: the spirit or mood of a particular period in history
items.explanation: A German word meaning 'time spirit', borrowed into English.
items.example: The film captured the zeitgeist of the 1960s.

items.definition: the highest point; the point in the sky directly overhead
items.example: The Roman Empire reached its zenith in the second century.
items.picture_idea: The sun at its highest point directly above a mountain

items.definition: full of energy and strong enthusiasm for a cause
items.example: The zealous volunteers cleaned the whole beach before noon.
items.picture_idea: Eager volunteers picking up litter on a beach

items.definition: the lowest point of something
items.explanation: The opposite of zenith. It comes from Arabic and also means the point in the sky directly below you.
items.example: Losing his job was the nadir of an awful year.
items.picture_idea: A graph line dropping to its lowest point

items.definition: stubbornly refusing to change your mind
items.example: The obstinate child refused to wear a coat even in the snow.
items.picture_idea: A child with folded arms shaking their head

items.definition: so strong that it can almost be felt; easy to notice
items.example: The tension in the room was palpable.
items.picture_idea: People sitting stiffly in a silent, tense room

items.definition: hopeful and optimistic, especially in a difficult situation
items.explanation: From Latin sanguis, 'blood'. Medieval people believed a lot of blood made someone cheerful.
items.example: Despite the delays, she remained sanguine about the project's success.
items.picture_idea: A smiling person looking up at a sunrise

items.definition: eager to argue or fight; aggressively defiant
items.example: The truculent customer shouted at everyone in the shop.
items.picture_idea: A scowling person with clenched fists

items.definition: charming and attractive in an innocent way
items.example: The little girl gave a winsome smile and won over the whole class.
items.picture_idea: A child with a bright, charming smile
